study.title: Psalm 90 The brevity of life and prayer for favor and firmness
study.overview: This psalm is a prayer attributed to Moses. He contrasts God's eternity with human frailty, recognizes that sin brings judgment and distress, and then turns I a lamentation into supplication: that the Lord teaches his people to live wisely, receive them with mercy, and confirm the work of his hands. The whole piece moves from the consciousness of mortality to the dependence of divine goodness.

outline.title: God eternal, transient humanity
outline.explanation: In the first verses, God is presented as a refuge and as the eternal Creator, before the mountains and the world. In contrast, humans are taken back to dust, and life is described as brief, fragile and transient, similar to sleep, current and grass that is born and dry rapid.

outline.title: The weight of sin and the need for wisdom
outline.explanation: Here the psalmist interprets the fragility of life in the light of divine wrath: human misery is not only natural, but also linked to guilt before God. Therefore, he asks for discernment to count the days correctly and reach a wise heart, that is, to live with awareness of the brevity of the life and seriousness of God.

outline.title: Request for mercy, joy and approval of God
outline.explanation: Prayer culminates in concrete requests: that the Lord turns, have compassion, satisfy his people with kindness, rejoice after days of distress, show his work and his glory, and finally put his liking over them, confirming the work of his hands.

study.context: The notes present the psalm as a prayer of Moses, the man of God. Matthew Henry relates the text to the desert period, when Israel suffered from unbelief, murmuring, and rebellion; but this appears as an interpretative hypothesis, not as a certain data of the text. It is also mentioned that the psalm was preserved and transmitted in the collection of sacred songs, and that its purpose is to teach the people to pray before the fragility of life and the necessity of divine restoration.
study.theology: The psalm affirms the absolute eternity of God and the radical finitude of the human being. The death, the affliction and brevity of the days are presented as realities that expose the fallen condition of humanity and the seriousness of the divine wrath against sin. At the same time, the text shows that the correct answer is not despair, but prayer: to ask for mercy, wisdom, joy, and God's favor. The final blessing is not only inner consolation; it includes the confirmation of human works, showing that effort without divine approval is insufficient. Thus, wise life is born of humility, repentance and continuous dependence on the Lord's pleasure.

scholarViews.insight: The psalm states that the unfortunate condition of the people demands to seek the light of the Lord; he alone makes his servants joyful and blesses future generations.
The request for God to teach to count the days is a prayer for sanctified use of affliction: to recognize the brevity of life to live wisely before God.
The repetition of the final request shows great emphasis: without the presence, approval and blessing of the Lord, until human work remains incomplete.

questions: How does the awareness that God is eternal changes the way I evaluate my own plans and concerns?
How have I counted my days: as if they were many, or with the wisdom of whom do you know that they are brief?
What work in my hands today needs, above all else, the approval and confirmation of the Lord?
study.practice: Choose a concrete area of your routine - family, work, studies or service in the church - and pray specifically how psalm teaches: recognize human limitation, ask mercy and ask God to confirm your effort. Then, organize this area more sobriety, avoiding acting as if you had unlimited time. End the day by thanking you for evidence of God's goodness and giving Him the results again.
study.uncertainty: It is not possible to safely affirm, only by the notes provided, the exact historical occasion of the composition of the psalm. The connection with the desert, the rebellion of Israel or with the reconstruction of the temple appears in the notes as an interpretation of commentators, not as textual certainty. Nor should one treat the discussion about the precise text as an undisputed fact.
